title: Beruriah and the Returned Jewels
text:
A Jewish midrash tells that Rabbi Meir was teaching in the house of study one Sabbath afternoon. While he was away, his two sons died at home. His wife Beruriah laid them on a bed and covered them with a sheet.

When Rabbi Meir came home after the Sabbath ended, he asked where his sons were. She said they had gone to the study house. He said he had looked for them there and not seen them. She brought him the cup for the blessing that ends the Sabbath, and he made it. Again he asked about his sons. She said they had gone somewhere and would come soon, and she gave him food.

When he had eaten, she said: "Rabbi, I have a question. Some time ago a man gave me something to keep for him. Now he has come back to claim it. Should I return it or not?" Meir said that of course a person must return a deposit to its owner.

She said she would not have returned it without his knowledge. Then she took him by the hand, led him up to the room and drew back the sheet. Meir began to weep: "My sons, my sons." Beruriah reminded him of his own words: did he not say a deposit must be returned to its owner? "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away."
lesson: Hard news can be given gently and in its time. Preparing someone you love for grief is itself an act of care.
people: Beruriah, Rabbi Meir, their two sons
caveat: The midrash is a late compilation, and the story is a pious legend rather than a historical record.
